payload.source_label: Equations (1.2) and (1.4) are mathematically identical after renaming the unknown and speed

contract.statement: In the one-dimensional scalar constant-coefficient setting, the advection equation q_t + ū q_x = 0 and the right-going one-way wave equation w_t + c w_x = 0, introduced with c > 0, have the same mathematical form under correspondence of the unknown and coefficient names. Their physical unknowns have different interpretations. The source explicitly calls the equations mathematically identical and suggests that similar mathematical and numerical techniques can handle the associated transport and wave phenomena (printed page 1, equation (1.2) and its context; printed page 2, equation (1.4), its context, and the paragraph beginning 'Mathematically').
assumptions: The compared equations are homogeneous, linear, scalar first-order equations in one spatial dimension within the constant-coefficient setting (printed page 1, equation (1.1) and scalar-case paragraph; printed page 2, paragraph following equation (1.4)).
The advection model has constant velocity ū (printed page 1, introduction to equation (1.2)).
The displayed wave model describes propagation to the right with c > 0 (printed page 2, opening paragraph and equation (1.4)).

The variables have different physical meanings: q measures a transported substance, while w combines pressure and particle velocity. The identity claim concerns their mathematical equations (printed page 1, introduction to equation (1.2); printed page 2, paragraph following equation (1.4) and identity paragraph).

The wave context distinguishes wave propagation speed from material-particle motion: the opening paragraph says the wave speed can be much larger than particle velocity (printed page 2, opening paragraph).
No initial conditions, boundary conditions, spatial boundary, or finite time interval are specified for the comparison (printed pages 1–2, displayed equations (1.2), (1.4), and identity paragraph).
quantifiers: x and t are the real spatial and temporal variables inherited from q : R × R → R^m; the present equations use the scalar case m = 1 (printed page 1, equation (1.1), its explanatory paragraph, and the scalar-case paragraph).
q(x,t) is the scalar advection unknown, interpreted as concentration or density (printed page 1, introduction to equation (1.2)).
ū is the constant real transport velocity (printed page 1, scalar-case paragraph and introduction to equation (1.2)).
w(x,t) is the scalar wave unknown, interpreted as an appropriate combination of pressure and particle velocity (printed page 2, equation (1.4) and its following paragraph).
c is the wave propagation speed, with c > 0 in the right-going model displayed in equation (1.4) (printed page 2, opening paragraph).
The identity sentence is a prose comparison of the displayed equations and contains no explicit universal or existential quantifiers (printed page 2, paragraph beginning 'Mathematically').
